A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same intermediate-image-encoder safety vulnerability. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title, terminology and substantially expanded scope.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix E report original layer-wise attack-success rates, toxicity scores and generated responses for LLaVA-1.5 and Llama 3.2.

after.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original vulnerability and alignment experiments, including LLaVA-NeXT results, human evaluations, visual-question-answering utility and over-refusal measurements.

M1.justification: The intermediate-layer projection procedure is retained and renamed ICET. The substantive addition is Layer-wise Clip-PPO: reward-guided optimization of the language backbone using a selected intermediate layer's embeddings, with clipped updates and KL regularization while freezing the image encoder and projector (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1).

E1.justification: The original 100-pair dataset is retained as Custom Prompts (CP). v2 adds broader harmful-query categories and natural, generated and noisy image inputs through RedTeam/Jailbreak-V28K, plus AdvBench-COCO evaluation and HH-RLHF reward-model training. VQA-v2 and safe XSTest prompts introduce distinct utility and over-refusal tasks (Section 4.1, Appendices B-C and J-K).

E2.justification: v1 compares default inference with intermediate-layer inference without evaluating an alternative alignment method. v2 adds one explicit alignment comparator, supervised fine-tuning, against L-PPO and the original model using RedTeam-2K training and CP testing (Appendix L, Tables 21-22).

E3.justification: v2 adds alignment train/test protocols and LLaVA-NeXT experiments, supplements mean ASR and toxicity with reward scores, VQA accuracy and refusal metrics, and drops maximum-ASR/toxicity summaries. New procedures include blinded, shuffled human judging by three annotators assessing 200 outputs each, and string-matched refusal evaluation on 150 safe XSTest prompts (Appendices H and K).

E4.justification: v2 adds utility-preservation and over-refusal analyses, a reported value-loss-coefficient sensitivity search, and strong, partial and failed mitigation case studies (Table 3, Appendices F-G and J-K). Conversely, the separate Llama Guard 2 and 3 robustness checks in v1 Figures 4-5 are no longer reported.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports aggregation across three human annotators and inter-annotator agreement using Fleiss' kappa, 0.8916 (Appendix H). Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive mitigation, utility, refusal and human-rated results. For example, CP average ASR is 64.62% before alignment, 37.96% after L-PPO and 55.14% after SFT (Tables 2 and 21); human-rated CP ASR changes from 50.21% to 16.74% (Table 15). The reported original early-layer LLaVA-1.5 AASR also differs between versions: 49.995% in v1 Table 2 versus 75.38% in v2 Table 2. This unexplained baseline revision cannot establish a same-setting performance gain or loss.

T1.justification: v1 provides forward-pass and metric equations without policy-improvement theory. v2 adds MDP definitions, a policy-improvement lemma, a cited performance bound and an argument extending it to L-PPO (Section 3.3), together with GAE derivations and a formal expected-regret interpretation of ICET (Appendices I and M).

C1.justification: The finding that intermediate encoder representations can compromise safety is retained. However, the abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the contribution from diagnosing this vulnerability to proposing L-PPO and claiming effective mitigation, theoretical improvement guarantees and preserved utility. These are substantive new claims beyond renaming the vulnerability ICET.

C2.justification: Beyond the retained OOD explanation, v2 explains disagreements between binary safety judgments and reward scores, discusses incoherent early-layer outputs and evaluator errors, and explicitly limits L-PPO to per-layer alignment. It also distinguishes partial improvements from failures and frames ICET as an architectural safety blind spot rather than a new jailbreak attack (Section 4.2, Appendices E-G).

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial implementation information absent from v1: LoRA rank 8, scaling 16 and dropout 0.05; Adam optimization; PPO epoch ranges; value-loss and adaptive-KL settings; PyTorch; and 2-4 NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPUs (Appendix F). It also supplies additional data-construction details and promises code, preprocessing scripts and aligned weights, without establishing their actual availability.

R1.justification: The research positioning expands from cross-modal attacks and LLM layer analysis to dynamic early exiting, preference optimization and multimodal RLHF, with new discussions of works by Bakhtiarnia, Xu, Uzkent, Schulman, Rafailov and Sun. The new gap analysis and discussion also connect the vulnerability to multilayer feature fusion, including DenseConnector (Sections 1-2 and 5).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten around ICET and mitigation. Background becomes a broader related-work and research-gap section; methodology and experiments gain substantial internal structure; and a discussion section is introduced. The appendices are reorganized into dedicated datasets, metrics, limitations, implementation, analysis and theory sections.

P2.justification: The overview is redrawn to incorporate L-PPO (v1 Figure 1 becomes v2 Figure 2), and v2 adds a first-page demonstration and three-panel before/after results. v1 Table 1 becomes the expanded, color-coded v2 Table 4. New human-evaluation, utility and SFT tables substantially change the presentation, while retained examples and Llama 3.2 plots are relocated or regrouped.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's narrow 100-pair exploratory evidence through broader evaluation, an implemented mitigation, an SFT comparison and blinded human validation. Utility controls address an important alternative explanation: VQA accuracy changes only from 48.73 to 48.23, while average safe-prompt refusal falls from 0.047 to 0.040 (Tables 3 and 20). Unexplained baseline revisions and the unsupported leap from a conditional policy bound to guaranteed safety improvement remain weaknesses, but the expanded empirical validation and implementation disclosure provide a substantial net quality gain.
